item.title: Spectral-Domain Information Geometry of Stationary Covariance Models: Gaussian and Elliptical Extensions
item.description: arXiv:2611.13037v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper develops an information-geometric framework for stationary covariance structures. We begin with the infinite-dimensional setting, where stationary covariance structures can be characterized without finite-window boundary effects. By formulating the covariance structure as a bilinear form on a suitable class of test functions, we establish its spectral representation and show how finite-dimensional Toeplitz covariance matrices arise as restrictions to nested observation subspaces. For zero-mean proper complex Gaussian wide-sense stationary (WSS) processes, we show that the normalized finite-dimensional Fisher information converges to a spectral-domain metric. In logarithmic spectral coordinates, this metric becomes the standard $L^2$ inner product, yielding an explicit Fisher--Rao distance that is also recovered as the asymptotic normalized affine-invariant Riemannian distance between Toeplitz covariance matrices. We then extend the framework to elliptical observation models by separating global covariance scale from shape. The shape Fisher information is orthogonal to radial nuisance directions and is characterized by a dimension- and radial-model-dependent coefficient. We derive a condition under which this coefficient converges to its Gaussian value as the observation dimension tends to infinity. The resulting limiting spectral-shape geometry is the centered $L^2$ geometry of log-spectra and is invariant to positive rescaling. Numerical experiments illustrate the theoretical convergence results and the recovery of the Gaussian shape coefficient.
item.dc:creator: Shu Yang, Dongying Li, Wenxian Yu

item.title: Adaptive local Fr\'echet regression with polyspherical predictors
item.description: arXiv:2611.13240v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study local Fr\'echet regression for responses taking values in a metric space and predictors on a product of spheres of possibly different dimensions. We propose local constant and local linear estimators with factor-specific bandwidths and establish uniform convergence rates. We select sphere factors by comparing cross-fitted prediction risks for the full and leave-one-factor-out models. The procedure consistently recovers the active factor set, and the selected local constant and local linear estimators attain the same uniform convergence rates as if the active factor set were known. For univariate Wasserstein responses supported on a common compact interval, the uniform rate holds without an entropy condition on the response space. Simulations with scalar and spherical responses and analyses of vessel speeds and drifter speed distributions illustrate the methods.
item.dc:creator: Chang Jun Im

item.title: Species sampling priors through exact augmentation
item.description: arXiv:2611.13323v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Discrete random probability measures are central to Bayesian nonparametric mixture modeling and clustering. We show that every proper species sampling process (SSP) admits an exact two-stage finite representation of its sampling law. An almost surely finite index selects an initial set of atoms, and a draw is then made with explicitly reweighted probabilities. A decreasing visibility schedule determines both the reweighting and the index law. Averaging the finite conditional measures over this law recovers each realized SSP on every measurable set. Reversing this identity yields a novel and general method for constructing SSP priors from an index distribution and finite allocation probabilities, rather than specifying the infinite weights directly. We characterize compatibility between prescribed index probabilities, schedules and induced weights, and develop new SSP priors with full weak support using light-tailed, heavy-tailed and multimodal index distributions with suitable priors on their parameters. Within this framework, we couple marginal index laws with conditional weight distributions to construct SSP priors whose weights are invariant under size-biased permutation in their defining order. An example of such family is identified as the normalization of the sum of a gamma completely random measure and an independent compound-Poisson measure with gamma jumps, naturally leading to explicit partition and predictive laws. The joint distribution of the selected label and the finite index also gives exact simulation and recursive reweighting for SSPs. Total-variation bounds and numerical illustrations distinguish prior specification, exact averaging and fixed-level approximation.
item.dc:creator: Rams\'es H. Mena, Christos Merkatas, Theodoros Nicoleris, Carlos E. Rodr\'iguez

item.title: Statistical Analysis of the Structure from Noise Phenomenon in Generalized Procrustes Problems
item.description: arXiv:2611.13546v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), observations are highly noisy, and scientists often use reference templates to guide matching, alignment, and averaging to reconstruct the molecular structure. However, these procedures can produce an output resembling the template even when the observations contain only noise, a phenomenon known as Einstein from noise (EfN). This phenomenon has attracted attention in statistics, where simplified observation models involving group actions have been studied to understand the resulting model bias. Characterizing the bias in the full cryo-EM pipeline remains challenging. We study template matching and averaging in the generalized orthogonal Procrustes problem, which provides an analytically tractable setting involving continuous orthogonal group action and lower-dimensional projections of ordered point clouds. We show that, for pure Gaussian noise, the mean of the aligned-and-averaged estimator admits the same left and right singular-vector bases as the template but its singular values may be distorted. This identifies the subspace structure imposed by the template even in the absence of signal. We characterize the singular values and bound their distortion, establish finite-sample operator-norm bounds, and give sufficient sample sizes for the population mean to dominate random fluctuations. In fact, this bias still exists under weak signals: when the template rank is at least the observation dimension, the change from the pure-noise mean is $O(\eta^2)$ in signal amplitude $\eta$. Our results provide an explicit characterization of model bias in a registration problem motivated by cryo-EM and show why averaging more observations can stabilize structure imposed by the template without removing the bias.
item.dc:creator: Jiayang Yin, Shuyang Ling

item.title: First-order asymptotic expansions for spectral convergence of normalized graph Laplacians constructed from samples on manifolds
item.description: arXiv:2611.13623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Under i.i.d. uniform sampling from a closed Riemannian manifold embedded in Euclidean space, we derive first-order asymptotic expansions for the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of symmetrically normalized graph Laplacians constructed via Gaussian kernels and provide concentration inequalities for the remainder terms. As a direct consequence, we establish the corresponding weak convergence results. Unlike most related works, our analysis does not impose a multiplicity-one assumption on the eigenvalues, thereby extending the applicability of the framework to general manifolds with potentially nontrivial eigenvalue multiplicities.
item.dc:creator: Eunseong Bae, Wolfgang Polonik

item.title: Asymptotic Bayes Optimality of Sparse Multiple Testing Procedures under One-Factor Dependence
item.description: arXiv:2611.13928v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study sparse multiple testing under a Gaussian two-group model with known one-factor covariance and centered Gaussian signals. We derive a first-order risk expansion for the observed-data Bayes Oracle, including a finite-dimensional loading average for heterogeneous loadings and an explicit limiting constant for homogeneous loadings. Under the stated factor-estimation and signal-calibration conditions, the homogeneous one-factor Oracle has strictly smaller leading risk than its independent-coordinate counterpart; observing the latent factor yields no further first-order reduction. We establish asymptotic Bayes optimality under sparsity (ABOS) for the Maximum Residual Down (MRD) step-down procedure with Gavrilov--Benjamini--Sarkar (GBS) stagewise calibration (MRD--GBS). Uniform control of residual errors along the rejection path permits comparison with a fixed factor-known rule without requiring the rejection paths to coincide. Fixed-residual versions of GBS and Benjamini--Hochberg (BH) attain the same leading risk. We also prove ABOS for the Bayesian Step-Down (BSD) rule when supplied with the true mixture, signal variance, covariance, and loss parameters; this is an Oracle-parameterized result. When the expected signal count grows faster than the logarithm of the reciprocal signal proportion, BSD and the observed-data Oracle disagree on several coordinates negligible in probability relative to the expected signal count, explaining BSD's near-Oracle behavior in companion simulations. The results cover diverging and bounded positive expected signal counts, including every fixed polynomial sparsity rate up to the bounded-count regime, under the stated calibrations. A fixed-dimension simulation illustrates absolute-risk behavior but does not establish ABOS.
item.dc:creator: Prasenjit Ghosh, Arijit Chakrabarti

item.title: Lengthscale Estimation for the Gaussian Kernel and Deterministic Response Functions
item.description: arXiv:2611.13930v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The uncertainty estimates Gaussian processes output rely on the chosen covariance kernel and its hyperparameters. We study the fixed-domain asymptotics of the maximum likelihood and cross-validation estimators of the lengthscale parameter of the popular infinitely smooth Gaussian kernel when the observations are produced by a fixed univariate response function. No theoretical results for Gaussian lengthscale estimation exist in this setting. We prove lower bounds on the lengthscale estimators that depend on the regularity of the response function, as measured by the rate of decay of its Fourier transform. If the response function lives in the Hilbert space of the Gaussian kernel with lengthscale $\ell$, the lower bounds have a straightforward dependency on $\ell$. For bandlimited functions and functions whose Fourier transforms decay as $\exp(-a \lvert \omega \rvert^\gamma)$ for $a > 0$ and $\gamma > 2$, we prove that the estimators blow up essentially at least as fast as $(\log n)^{(\gamma-2)/(2\gamma)}$ in the number of data points, $n$. Bandlimited functions are identified with $\gamma = \infty$. Unlike analogous results for finitely smooth Mat\'ern kernels, our results make no assumptions on the geometry of the observation points. Numerical experiments illustrate the results.
item.dc:creator: Subhendu Pramanick, Toni Karvonen

item.title: A linear programming approach to finite copula interpolation
item.description: arXiv:2611.14008v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider exact and interval-valued interpolation of multivariate copulas at arbitrary finite configurations in the unit cube. We first characterize when the prescribed data are compatible with a quasi-copula and derive explicit extremal quasi-copula envelopes. The copula interpolation problem is thereby reduced to a copula sandwich problem between these envelopes. Restricting them to the canonical rectangular grid generated by the data coordinates yields a finite linear feasibility system whose elementary-volume constraints are encoded by a cell--vertex incidence matrix. Farkas' lemma then identifies the criterion of Omladi\v{c} and Stopar with an explicit certificate of infeasibility. Although this criterion is indexed by infinitely many formal cell combinations, we show that it suffices to test finitely many vertices of a sign-polytopal subdivision. We also extend the construction to $k$-increasing discrete quasi-copulas for $2\leq k\leq d$.
item.dc:creator: Matja\v{z} Omladi\v{c}, Martin Vuk, Alja\v{z} Zalar

item.title: On the geometry of Gaussian Mean Shift Detection
item.description: arXiv:2611.14264v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the problem of detecting a shift in the mean of a standard Gaussian random vector, where the direction of the shift belongs to an arbitrary subset $T$ of the Euclidean unit sphere. We introduce a correlation functional $\kappa(T)$ and establish a general lower bound on the detection radius in terms of this functional. We identify regularity conditions under which this lower bound is optimal up to an absolute constant. As an application, we recover some well-known results in the literature such as the detection radius for $s$-sparse unit vectors.
item.dc:creator: Pedro Abdalla, Grigoris Paouris, Roman Vershynin

item.title: Smoothed Least-Absolute Conditional Multidimensional Scaling via Iteratively Reweighted Majorization
item.description: arXiv:2611.14345v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conditional multidimensional scaling combines latent coordinates with observed covariates to fit pairwise dissimilarities. We develop a smoothed l1 formulation using the shifted Charbonnier loss. We prove residualwise sharpness of the quadratic loss majorizer, monotonicity, compact containment, and stationarity of noncollapsed accumulation points. A uniform additive bound quantifies approximation to exact least-absolute conditional stress. The experiments use paired contamination, separately calibrated loss parameters, combined-configuration recovery, and direct checks of the theorem's inequalities.
item.dc:creator: Xiao Ling

item.title: Generalized Cram\'er-Rao Inequalities Associated with $(h,\tau)$-Divergence and $(h,\tau)$-Exponential Family
item.description: arXiv:2611.14346v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence and exponential family have laid the foundation for information geometry and have been widely generalized. Using Eguchi's theory, the Fisher information metric can be derived from the KL divergence. Based on this metric, Amari and Nagaoka established an information-geometric proof of the classical Cram\'er-Rao (CR) inequality for finite-support models. Among the various generalizations of the KL divergence, this paper focuses on the $(h,\tau)$-divergence and establishes the associated CR inequality, referred to as the $(h,\tau)$-CR inequality, using information geometry. We also provide a proof of this inequality based on the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, thereby extending its applicability to models with more general support sets. Under suitable regularity conditions, equality holds in the classical CR inequality if and only if the underlying family is exponential. However, for the $(h,\tau)$-CR inequality, this property does not generally extend to the $(h,\tau)$-exponential family. We therefore establish an attainable CR inequality for this family. This new inequality extends the attainment result of the classical CR inequality by the sufficient statistic of the exponential family to the $(h,\tau)$-exponential family.
item.dc:creator: Satyajit Dhadumia

item.title: Analytic and optimized approximations to the median of the gamma distribution
item.description:
arXiv:2611.14429v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The median $
u_\Gamma(\alpha)$ of the gamma distribution has no closed form, but its behavior at both ends is known: it is asymptotic to $2^{-1/\alpha}e^{-\gamma}$ (with $\gamma$ being the Euler-Mascheroni constant) as the shape parameter $\alpha 	o 0$, and approaches $\alpha - 1/3$ as $\alpha 	o \infty$. We write approximations as interpolations $(1 - g)
u_0 + g
u_\infty$ between two elementary-function bounds or approximations, each exact in one limit, with an interpolator $g(\alpha)$ going from 0 to 1, and compare three such forms: a first one between previously proven bounds, a second ending in an approximation from the beta median that is exact at $\alpha = 1$ but does not quite approach $\alpha - 1/3$ as $\alpha 	o \infty$, and a third one, between bounds proved here, that corrects the large-$\alpha$ end of the second. For each form, the ideal interpolator's slope at 0, approach to 1, and value at $\alpha = 1$ are derived in closed form. Rational interpolators with every coefficient set in closed form from these properties, with no numerical fitting, reach a worst relative error of 0.0011 over all $\alpha > 0$, with absolute error below 0.0002. Fitting some of these or other coefficients numerically to minimize the worst absolute-or-relative error then trades accuracy against complexity: the Pareto frontier reaches 0.000087 with two fitted constants and 0.000041 with five, and from two on uses degree-4 rationals of the second form with no $\alpha^2$ term in the numerator. The proofs that the end functions of the first and third forms are bounds are machine-checked in Lean 4.
item.dc:creator: Richard F. Lyon

item.title: Nonparametric Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Mixtures of Logistic Regressions
item.description: arXiv:2611.14445v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mixtures of logistic regressions provide a flexible framework for modeling binary responses, extending standard logistic regression to accommodate unobserved heterogeneity while retaining an interpretable regression structure. In this paper, we study such models with an unspecified mixing distribution. We analyze a sieve nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE) and derive nonasymptotic bounds on the estimation error of the resulting mixture regression function under both fixed and random designs. Our results reveal an explicit tradeoff between statistical estimation error and the approximation error induced by the sieve radius, from which we derive convergence rates under several tail conditions on the mixing distribution. For computation, we propose a finite-particle algorithm that approximates the sieve NPMLE by optimizing the locations and weights of a finitely supported mixing distribution. The method offers numerical advantages over existing algorithms and comes with rigorous convergence guarantees. For any fixed dataset, we establish global convergence of the likelihood to the restricted NPMLE value when the number of particles exceeds a finite threshold. When the true mixing distribution is finitely supported, we further establish uniform global convergence guarantees and derive error bounds that separate algorithmic and statistical errors. Our analysis also yields a denoising bound for the mixing distribution and an identifiability result that complements existing results in the literature.
item.dc:creator: Muheng Li, Peize Zhang, Xin Bing

item.title: Causal Learning with Invalid Instruments for High-dimensional Imaging Responses
item.description: arXiv:2611.13187v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large-scale neuroimaging studies provide high-dimensional imaging phenotypes for understanding brain-related diseases and their causal relations with biological risk factors. While instrumental variable (IV) methods can address unmeasured confounding in such observational data, existing IV methods face significant limitations when applied to high-dimensional imaging data, particularly in handling large-scale data and leveraging the intrinsic spatial structure of images. To address these challenges, we propose High-dimensional Functional-imaging Instrumental Variable Estimation (Hi-FIVE), a novel framework for estimating spatially varying causal effects when a majority of the candidate instruments may be locally invalid. We first establish identifiability conditions under which the spatial continuity of the causal effect surface propagates identification from regions where valid instruments form a plurality into regions where they do not, provided that invalid-IV effects switch on non-smoothly. Motivated by this result, Hi-FIVE combines penalized multivariate splines over triangulations for the causal surface and region-wise penalties for spatially localized invalid-IV effects, under an anchor constraint that keeps at least one relevant instrument valid on every simplex. A distributed algorithm parallelizes the computation over simplices for two- and three-dimensional images. We study the asymptotic properties of Hi-FIVE, establish consistency and pointwise asymptotic normality, and construct bootstrap-calibrated simultaneous confidence regions whose finite-sample coverage is evaluated through simulations. Hi-FIVE is illustrated with an analysis of the effect of phosphorylated tau on FDG-PET imaging in the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, interpreted under the stated IV assumptions.
item.dc:creator: Yiting Wang, Chunlin Li, Shan Yu, Lily Wang

item.title: Continuous Horizon Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2611.13228v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-horizon forecasting has been dominated by discrete forecast strategies that treat model outputs as fixed-vectors or recurrently create them. In this paper, we introduce the Continuous Horizon (CH) strategy that generalizes upon recursive, direct, and multi-step strategies by redefining forecasts as a continuous operator and the forecast horizon as a query variable rather than an index. We present the theoretical foundations for the CH strategy, a Universal Operator Approximation Theorem, and a continuous-horizon bias-variance decomposition that formally proves the estimation variance improvements of CH over the discrete strategies. We validate the CH strategy empirically through a simulation study, and on 16 large-scale datasets from the M-series benchmark, showing how CH achieves competitive RMSE accuracy, while uniquely enabling parallel inference, targeted horizon querying, and interpolation and extrapolation across unseen horizons.
item.dc:creator: Malcolm Wolff, Elliott Zackrone, Souhaib Ben Taieb, Michael W. Mahoney, Kin G. Olivares

item.title: Time Series Change Point Detection with Gaussian Processes
item.description: arXiv:2611.13295v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper proposes a novel general Gaussian process framework for change point detection in time series. A change is defined as an alteration of the hyperparameters of the Gaussian process prior. We formulate the problem in the context of statistical hypothesis testing and demonstrate its performance over both offline and online multiple change points detection. The approach provides theoretical guaranties of its performance. An important advantage of the developed framework is that it does not need a detailed specification of the time series function before and after a change. The hyperparameter values are learned from the data. Comprehensive evaluation of the proposed framework is provided both on synthetic and real data and its efficiency is demonstrated.
item.dc:creator: Olga Isupova, Danil Kuzin, Fredrik Gustafsson, Lyudmila Mihaylova

item.title: Regression Modeling for the Bloc Basu Bivariate Exponential Distribution: Marginal and Conditional Means
item.description: arXiv:2611.13433v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The bivariate absolutely continuous exponential distribution introduced by \citet{block1974continuous} provides a model for dependent lifetimes in reliability and survival analysis. Its marginal means depend jointly and nonlinearly on the rate parameters, which complicates regression modeling and the interpretation of covariate effects on these means. In this paper, we develop two regression approaches based on a region-wise multivariate exponential-family representation. In the full-distribution approach, link functions relate the cumulant derivatives in a fixed reference region to linear predictors. These derivatives do not directly equal the marginal means, which are instead probability-weighted combinations of the regional derivatives. This relationship allows covariate effects on the marginal means to be examined. Likelihood derivatives are obtained through the chain rule, and the regression coefficients are estimated by maximum likelihood. The rate parameter estimates are then recovered through the inverse link functions and an explicit inverse mapping, with the admissible solution selected to ensure positive rates. As an alternative, we propose regression models based on the normalized conditional distribution within each region. In this setting, the cumulant derivatives coincide with the conditional means, allowing covariates to be linked directly to these means. Both approaches are evaluated through a simulation study.
item.dc:creator: Osama Idais, Eric Nyarko, Ola Alkhuffash

item.title: Sufficient Dimension Reduction with Multimodal Predictor Objects
item.description: arXiv:2611.13460v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the regression of a scalar response $Y$ on a Euclidean predictor $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^p$ and a random predictor object $\mathcal{Z}$ in a general metric space under arbitrary structural dependence. We introduce a joint sufficient dimension reduction $(\mathbf{B}^\top\mathbf{X}, \mathcal{G}_Z)$ constructed via a sequential conditional independence framework, which differs fundamentally from the ordinary central subspace of $Y \mid \mathbf{X}$. Methodologically, $\mathcal{Z}$ is embedded into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, and a regularized kernel-response envelope model extracts a finite-dimensional reduction of the feature map. Partial adaptive estimation then recovers the Euclidean reduction conditional on the first-stage coordinates. We establish root-$n$ consistency rates for the first-stage envelope subspace under a shrinking regularizer, alongside large-sample consistency for the second-stage Euclidean subspace estimator. Simulations and two real-data applications illustrate the utility and flexibility of the proposed method.
item.dc:creator: Abdul-Nasah Soale

item.title: Measuring Kaplan--Meier Overestimation Under Competing Risks: Event Ordering, Quantification, and Exact Inference
item.description: arXiv:2611.14457v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Competing risks arise when individuals may experience multiple mutually exclusive event types. Competing events are frequently treated as censoring and analysed using Kaplan--Meier (KM) methods, which overestimate real-world event risks. While the existence of KM overestimation is well known, its determinants, magnitude, and inferential properties remain poorly characterised. We develop a nonparametric framework that treats competing risks overestimation as a statistical quantity in its own right. We show that competing event frequency alone is insufficient to characterise KM overestimation and develop an event ordering theory describing how temporal event allocation influences overestimation. Based on these results, we derive a closed-form Total Overestimation Diagnostic (TOD) that quantifies total KM overestimation directly from routine survival analysis output. We establish exact error equivalence results for both cause-specific and total overestimation. In particular, Product Limit Error Equivalence shows that inference for TOD reduces exactly to ordinary overall survival estimation. Simulation experiments validate the theoretical results and show that independent censoring primarily affects precision rather than overestimation magnitude. Across six benchmark competing risks datasets, cause-specific overestimation is characterised by both total overestimation and temporal event allocation. These results provide a practical framework for assessing competing risks relevance and determining when cumulative incidence methods should be preferred to na\"ive KM risks. The proposed framework transforms competing risks overestimation from a qualitative warning into a measurable quantity that can be routinely quantified, interpreted, and incorporated into reporting practice.
item.dc:creator: Ferran Espuny-Pujol

item.title: A Theory of Cross-Validation Variance
item.description: arXiv:2611.14463v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cross-validation estimates predictive performance by repeatedly splitting the data into training and validation sets, fitting the model on the first and evaluating it on the second. Every observation influences the estimate in two roles, through its own evaluation when it is held out and through the models it helps fit when it trains. The random splits determine its weight in each role. From this representation, we prove an exact finite-sample identity for the variance of the cross-validated estimate. For a given splitting scheme with a common training set size, the variance is a function of these weights, with constants of the model, the metric, and the population. It covers metrics averaged over observations, such as mean squared error, and over case--control pairs, such as the AUC. The identity shows which schemes to use. The variance decomposes into sampling variance, which depends only on the training size, and variance due to the random fold splitting, which arises when the weights change from one draw of the splits to the next. K-fold cross-validation, whose weights are equal across observations by design, is therefore variance optimal at first order; Monte Carlo and bootstrap cross-validation are not. The first-order variance of K-fold does not depend on K, and under reasonable conditions on the model leave-one-out has the smallest variance of any K-fold scheme. For the AUC the same holds for leave-pair-out, which evaluates every case--control pair. Finally, we show the cross-validated estimate is asymptotically normal with the identity's full variance. Together, these results provide a general theoretical foundation for inference on cross-validated performance and establish principles for selecting variance-optimal cross-validation designs.
item.dc:creator: Nathaniel S. O'Connell, Jaime L. Speiser

item.title: Bayesian inverse problems and epidemic-threshold uncertainty for a heterogeneous SIS reaction-diffusion model
item.description: arXiv:2611.14468v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study Bayesian inference of persistence from early observations of a heterogeneous susceptible--infected--susceptible (SIS) reaction--diffusion model with standard incidence. We show that the leading prevalence dynamics depend on the unknown coefficients only through the difference between the transmission and recovery rates and the infected diffusivity. The same pair determines the principal eigenvalue whose sign governs persistence, so early prevalence can inform the threshold even when the individual rates remain uncertain. We prove global weak well-posedness and quantitative parameter stability for the SIS system and use the resulting observation-map estimates to establish Bayesian well-posedness. For an initial infection of size $\varepsilon$, we derive a uniform second-order expansion that describes how the separate rates enter prevalence. Incidence depends explicitly on transmission at leading order. When the noise standard deviation is proportional to $\varepsilon$, we prove $O(\varepsilon)$ convergence in Hellinger distance of the nonlinear posteriors to their low-prevalence limits for both prevalence alone and joint prevalence and incidence data. We bound the principal eigenvalue using the growth rate of the infected $L^2$ norm between two times. This rate gives a lower bound for the full nonlinear system, and the upper bound separates spatial transients from nonlinear saturation. Uniform spectral estimates and bounds on infection size and measurement error give sufficient conditions for persistence and extinction. We also bound the error in posterior persistence probabilities under forward and eigenvalue approximation, accounting for posterior mass near the threshold. Numerical examples illustrate threshold inference and the predicted \(O(\varepsilon)\) convergence of the nonlinear posteriors to their low-prevalence limits in Hellinger distance.
item.dc:creator: Duc-Lam Duong

item.title: Nonparametric estimation of linear multiplier for SDEs driven by generalized stochastic volatility
item.description: arXiv:2412.00005v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the problem of nonparametric estimation of the linear multiplier function $\theta(t)$ for processes satisfying stochastic differential equations of the type $$dX_t= \theta(t)X_t dt+ \epsilon\; \sigma(t,X_t,Y_t)dW_t, X_0=x_0, 0 \leq t \leq T$$ based on the observation of the process $\{X_t, 0\leq t \leq T\}$ and investigate the asymptotic properties of the estimator as the small noise $\epsilon$ tends to zero. Here $\{W_t, t\geq 0\}$ is the standard Brownian motion and $\{Y_t, t\geq 0\}$ is a process adapted to the filtration generated by the Brownian motion.
item.dc:creator: B. L. S Prakasa Rao

item.title: Do we really need the Rademacher complexities?
item.description: arXiv:2502.15118v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the fundamental problem of learning with respect to the squared loss in a convex class. In the subgaussian setting, the sharpest known sample complexity bounds are characterised via fixed points associated with the limiting gaussian process. In more general settings (for example, heavier-tailed scenarios) the state-of-the-art bounds rely on localised Rademacher complexities, which are often difficult to control and can be considerably larger than their limiting gaussian counterparts. We show that if one has access to coarse information on the covariance structure of the underlying class, it is possible to derive an upper bound on the sample complexity that matches the state-of-the-art rates in the gaussian setting---even in heavy-tailed regimes. As a consequence, under rather minimal assumptions, learning problems that share the same $L_2$-structure---even those involving heavy-tailed distributions---admit the same upper bound on the sample complexity as if the problem were fully gaussian. This constitutes the first universality result for general convex learning problems. The proof is based on a novel learning procedure, and its performance is studied by combining optimal mean estimation techniques for real-valued random variables with Talagrand's generic chaining method.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Bartl, Shahar Mendelson

item.title: Random tree Besov priors: Data-driven regularisation parameter selection
item.description: arXiv:2601.12957v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a data-driven algorithm for automatically selecting the wavelet density parameters in Bayesian inversion under random tree Besov priors. One of the key challenges in Bayesian inversion is the construction of priors that are both expressive and computationally feasible. Random tree Besov priors, introduced in \cite{Kekkonen2023}, provide a flexible framework for capturing local regularity properties and sparsity patterns in a wavelet basis. In this paper, we extend this approach by introducing a hierarchical model that enables data-driven selection of the wavelet density parameter, allowing the regularisation strength to adapt across scales while retaining computational efficiency. We focus on nonparametric regression and also present preliminary plug-and-play results for a deconvolution problem.
item.dc:creator: Hanne Kekkonen, Andreas Tataris

item.title: Minimax Optimal Estimation of Transport-Growth Pairs in Unbalanced Optimal Transport
item.description: arXiv:2605.08705v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Unbalanced optimal transport extends classical optimal transport to measures with different total masses, but statistical guarantees for estimation of the transport map and the growth map remain limited. We study unbalanced optimal transport with quadratic cost and Kullback-Leibler marginal penalties and argue that the natural target of estimation is a transport-growth pair. Consequently, we develop two estimators for the transport-growth pair under two setups: a nearest-neighbor estimator for transporting between general densities, and a kernel-based estimator for transporting between smooth densities. We prove that the kernel-based estimator achieves the minimax optimal rate up to a logarithmic factor by deriving a matching lower bound on the minimax risk. Our main technical contribution is a reduction of estimation to a stability bound on the unbalanced optimal transport value. This bound controls the transport map and growth map risks through the duality gap of the true dual potentials for the estimated measures. These results provide a statistical foundation for estimation of the transport-growth pair in unbalanced optimal transport.
item.dc:creator: Donlapark Ponnoprat, Noboru Isobe, Masaaki Imaizumi

item.title: Asymptotic Theory for Sample Canonical Direction Alignment in High-Dimensional Spiked CCA
item.description: arXiv:2606.09153v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies the asymptotic behavior of sample canonical directions in a finite-rank spiked high-dimensional canonical correlation analysis model under a Gaussian population assumption. Under the asymptotic regime in which the dimensions of the two data blocks grow proportionally with the sample size, sample canonical directions are generally not consistent estimators of their population counterparts, even when the corresponding sample canonical correlations separate from the bulk spectrum. To quantify directional recovery, we investigate the squared alignment between a sample canonical direction and its associated population direction. For a supercritical simple population spike, we establish an explicit nonzero deterministic limit for the squared alignment. In contrast, for population non-spikes, we show that the alignment with the corresponding population signal directions vanishes asymptotically. Thus, the same phase transition that governs eigenvalue separation also marks a transition in directional recovery. For a supercritical simple spike, we further prove a central limit theorem for its fluctuations around the deterministic limit, with an explicit asymptotic variance expressed through deterministic limits of resolvent trace functionals. To make the theoretical quantities computable from data, we further construct plug-in estimators for both the deterministic alignment limit and the asymptotic variance by inverting the deterministic outlier eigenvalue map, and prove their consistency. Numerical simulations and a real-data illustration support the theoretical results and demonstrate how the proposed estimators assess the recovery quality of sample canonical directions.
item.dc:creator: Zhangni Pu, Xiaozhuo Zhang, Jiang Hu

item.title: $P$-stationary structural equation modeling: Causal effect identification under temporally incomplete observations
item.description: arXiv:2611.02252v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Causal modeling of discrete-time processes often involves the assumption that the modeled processes are stationary. A general class of linear causal models for discrete-time stationary processes are structural equation processes (SEP), which generalize the well known structural equation model for i.i.d. observations. In this paper, we extend the SEP model from stationary to $P$-stationary processes, which are non-stationary processes whose $P$-periodically sampled subprocesses are jointly stationary. We will use this model to approach the problem of causal effect identification under temporally incomplete observations from a graphical modeling perspective. To have a notion of generic identifiability, we restrict our analysis to $P$-stationary structural vector autoregressive (SVAR) processes, which are SVAR processes whose underlying coefficients can vary $P$-periodically over time. Our findings allow to detect, in any given temporally incomplete observational setting, if a set of $P$-periodic instrumental subprocesses qualifies to identify a causal effect between $P$-periodic subprocesses, and if this is the case, that effect admits an explicit expression as a rational function evaluated at the observational spectral density.
item.dc:creator: Nicolas-Domenic Reiter

item.title: A Note on the Cut-Locus-Corrected Fr\'echet Mean Central Limit Theorem
item.description: arXiv:2611.07956v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We record three observations concerning \cite{HLW24}. First, the proof of its Theorem~1 yields the population linearization (13)--(14) at \textit{any critical point} of the Fr\'echet function $F_\mu$, under its remaining geometric and measure-theoretic assumptions; neither \textit{isolation} nor a \textit{nonsingular} Hessian of $F_\mu$ is needed. Second, its Theorem~2 is given a shorter proof by applying the M-estimator theorem \cite[Theorem~5.23, pp.~53--54]{vdV98} to negative squared distance in normal coordinates, as opposed to the Donsker argument used there. Third, the above shorter route also helps us establish a CLT for a measurable selection of strict local empirical Fr\'echet mean with positive definite Hessian, with the cut locus correction, relaxing the assumptions of uniqueness or global minimality, as in \cite{HLW24}. Numerical experiments at the end show the agreement of the Hessian of the Fr\'echet function at \textit{local} Fr\'echet means with the (signed) sum of the expected Hessian of the squared distance function and the cut locus correction there.
item.dc:creator: Susovan Pal

item.title: Minimax designs and estimators for causal inference under network interference
item.description: arXiv:2611.08560v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a design-based minimax theory for linear causal estimands under interference. We study the minimax risks of three problems: optimizing an estimator under a fixed design, optimizing an estimator and a design from a restricted class, or optimizing both over all designs. In each problem, we study the minimax risk over all estimators and over design-unbiased estimators separately. We allow any correctly specified exposure mapping, including the identity. Our theory represents causal inference under interference as a constrained sampling design on an expanded finite population of $\sum_i d_i$ potential outcomes, where $d_i$ is the number of exposure levels attainable by unit $i$. We describe the constrained sampling design by a weighted sampling hypergraph: its vertices are the potential outcomes, its hyperedges are the maximal sets of potential outcomes that can be jointly sampled under feasible treatment assignments, and its weights are induced by the randomization design. We show that the minimax risks of the fixed-design, restricted-design, and all-design problems depend, respectively, on the weighted hypergraph induced by the design, the collection of weighted hypergraphs attainable within the restricted class, and the unweighted hypergraph. Our Bayes lower bounds compare potential-outcome tables that differ on jointly missing sets of potential outcomes: joint-missingness probabilities govern the lower bounds over all estimators, whereas the corresponding odds govern the lower bounds over unbiased estimators. We illustrate the theory for average treatment effects without interference, saturation designs under partial interference, total, direct, and contagion effects under neighborhood interference, and bipartite dose-response contrasts. The upper and lower bounds match in several settings.
item.dc:creator: Vishesh Karwa, Edoardo M. Airoldi

item.title: Coverage and shape of conformal highest-density sets: A minimax theory
item.description: arXiv:2611.11909v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study conditional coverage and geometric efficiency of conformal highest-density sets. The excess volume of such a set over the conditional highest-density set, the smallest set with the required conditional coverage, splits into a coverage error and an excess mass. We show that, among procedures whose volume is accurate up to a constant, the coverage error has the minimax rate of nonparametric regression on the covariate, and that the excess mass has the squared minimax rate of conditional density estimation. The usual split conformal construction calibrates these sets with a single threshold, which corrects the bias of the density estimate only on average over the covariate. We prove that its coverage error can then be of the order of the slower density rate. We therefore propose two-stage calibration, which estimates the coverage of the super-level sets of a density estimate by a regression on the covariate and uses this estimated coverage as the conformity score. Since these sets are fixed at each covariate value, their coverage is as smooth as the conditional density, and, under mild regularity conditions, the coverage error attains the regression rate even when the density estimate is inconsistent. The shape of the set still depends on the accuracy of the density estimate: sup-norm accuracy controls it at the minimax excess-mass rate, whereas accuracy in an integrated norm, even of minimax order, does not. With a local polynomial density estimate, two-stage calibration attains both minimax rates up to logarithmic factors. Simulations and an application to bike-sharing demand illustrate the results.
item.dc:creator: Ilsang Ohn

item.title: BONuS: Multiple multivariate testing with a data-adaptive test statistic
item.description: arXiv:2106.15743v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose a new adaptive empirical Bayes framework, the Bag-Of-Null-Statistics (BONuS) procedure, for multiple testing where each hypothesis testing problem is itself multivariate or nonparametric. BONuS is an adaptive and interactive knockoff-type method that helps improve the testing power while controlling the false discovery rate (FDR). The BONuS procedure is closely connected to many existing FDR-controlling methods, such as the counting knockoffs procedure and Benjamini-Hochberg procedure with conformal p-values. Contrary to procedures that start with a $p$-value for each hypothesis, BONuS analyzes the entire data set to adaptively estimate an optimal $p$-value transform based on an empirical Bayes model. Moreover, it can iteratively refine the model fit by peeling off synthetic null statistics to reduce noise in a highly adaptively way. Our method controls FDR in finite samples even if the empirical Bayes model is incorrect or the estimation is poor. An extension, the Double BONuS procedure, validates the empirical Bayes model to guard against power loss due to model misspecification. We demonstrate the power gain of BONuS procedure on multi-trait GWAS, asset pricing, and LLM evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Zhifei Li, Chiao-Yu Yang, Lihua Lei, Nhat Ho, William Fithian

item.title: The Star Geometry of Critic-Based Regularizer Learning
item.description: arXiv:2408.16852v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Variational regularization is a classical technique to solve statistical inference tasks and inverse problems, with modern data-driven approaches parameterizing regularizers via deep neural networks showcasing impressive empirical performance. Recent works along these lines learn task-dependent regularizers. This is done by integrating information about the measurements and ground-truth data in an unsupervised, critic-based loss function, where the regularizer attributes low values to likely data and high values to unlikely data. However, there is little theory about the structure of regularizers learned via this process and how it relates to the two data distributions. To make progress on this challenge, we initiate a study of optimizing critic-based loss functions to learn regularizers over a particular family of regularizers: gauges (or Minkowski functionals) of star-shaped bodies. This family contains regularizers that are commonly employed in practice and shares properties with regularizers parameterized by deep neural networks. We specifically investigate critic-based losses derived from variational representations of statistical distances between probability measures. By leveraging tools from star geometry and dual Brunn-Minkowski theory, we illustrate how these losses can be interpreted as dual mixed volumes that depend on the data distribution. This allows us to derive exact expressions for the optimal regularizer in certain cases. Finally, we identify which neural network architectures give rise to such star body gauges and when do such regularizers have favorable properties for optimization. More broadly, this work highlights how the tools of star geometry can aid in understanding the geometry of unsupervised regularizer learning.
item.dc:creator: Oscar Leong, Eliza O'Reilly, Yong Sheng Soh

item.title: Large Deviations Principle for Bures-Wasserstein Barycenters
item.description: arXiv:2409.11384v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We prove the large deviations principle for empirical Bures-Wasserstein barycenters of independent, identically-distributed samples of covariance matrices and covariance operators. As an application, we explore some consequences of our results for the phenomenon of dimension-free concentration of measure for Bures-Wasserstein barycenters. Our theory reveals a novel notion of exponential tilting in the Bures-Wasserstein space, which, in analogy with Cram\'er's theorem in the Euclidean case, solves the relative entropy projection problem under a constraint on the barycenter. Notably, this method of proof is easy to adapt to other geometric settings of interest; with the same method, we obtain large deviations principles for empirical barycenters in Riemannian manifolds and the univariate Wasserstein space, and we obtain large deviations upper bounds for empirical barycenters in the general multivariate Wasserstein space. In fact, our results are the first known large deviations principles for Fr\'echet means in any non-linear metric space.
item.dc:creator: Adam Quinn Jaffe, Leonardo V. Santoro

item.title: Posterior Contraction Rates for Sparse Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks in Anisotropic Besov Spaces
item.description: arXiv:2605.11652v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study posterior contraction rates for sparse Bayesian Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (KANs) over anisotropic Besov spaces, providing a statistical foundation for KANs from a Bayesian point of view. We show that sparse Bayesian KANs equipped with spike-and-slab-type sparsity priors attain a near-minimax posterior contraction rate. In particular, the contraction rate depends on the intrinsic anisotropic smoothness of the underlying function. Moreover, by placing a hyperprior on a single model-size parameter, the resulting posterior adapts to unknown anisotropic smoothness and still achieves the corresponding near-minimax rate. A distinctive feature of our results, compared with those for standard multilayer perceptrons, is that the KAN depth can be kept fixed: owing to the expressive power of learnable spline edge functions, the required approximation complexity is controlled through the network width, the range and size of the spline grid, and parameter sparsity. Our analysis develops theoretical tools tailored to sparse spline-edge architectures, including approximation and complexity bounds for Bayesian KANs. We then extend to compositional Besov spaces and show that the contraction rates depend on layerwise smoothness and effective dimension of the underlying compositional structure, thereby effectively avoiding the curse of dimensionality. Together, these results advance the theoretical understanding of Bayesian neural networks and establish rigorous Bayesian guarantees for KANs.
item.dc:creator: Jeunghun Oh, Jaeyong Lee, Lizhen Lin, Kyeongwon Lee

item.title: Factor Augmented High-Dimensional SGD
item.description: arXiv:2605.19291v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is a fundamental optimization algorithm widely used in modern machine learning. In this paper, we propose Factor-Augmented SGD (FSGD), a new optimization method that leverages latent factor representations in high-dimensional learning tasks. Unlike standard two-stage dimension reduction approaches that rely on offline representation learning and full data storage, a key novelty of FSGD is that it operates purely on streaming data, making it scalable to large-scale and high-dimensional problems. Furthermore, we establish the first theoretical framework that explicitly incorporates latent factor estimation error into the analysis of SGD, and provide moment convergence in $\ell^s$ norm under decaying step sizes and mini-batch updates. Our results provide a new foundation for employing SGD reliably and scalably in high-dimensional machine learning systems.
item.dc:creator: Shubo Li, Yuefeng Han, Xiufan Yu

item.title: Uniform Central Limit Theorems for Degree Distributions of Sparse Graphon Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.06892v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The degree distribution is among the most basic summaries of a network, yet no functional limit theorem for the empirical degree distribution of graphon models has been available, even for dense, bounded graphons, for which only finite-dimensional results were known. We study the empirical degree distribution of sparse $L^p$ graphon models, allowing unbounded kernels and hence heavy-tailed degrees. For graphons whose latent expected degrees have a density, we prove a finite-dimensional central limit theorem whenever $n\rho_n/\log n\to\infty$ and $n\rho_n^{2+\beta}\to0$, where $\rho_n$ is the sparsity level and the kernel has $2+\beta$ moments for some $\beta>0$; the limiting covariance coincides with that of the dense case. Under additional local regularity, we establish a functional central limit theorem on compact intervals in the interior of the support. Under tail regularity and a stronger sparsity condition, we prove that uniformity extends to unbounded intervals. We also show that uniform limits fail at atoms of the degree distribution, for instance in stochastic block models. The analysis rests on an exact multilinear representation of the conditional degree distribution, which identifies its Hoeffding decomposition without Edgeworth expansions, combined with a lattice version of Billingsley's tightness criterion and moment inequalities of Efron-Stein type.
item.dc:creator: Robert Lunde, Soumendra Lahiri
